SportsTab.title: Joshua vs Fury: Where does AJ's 'chaotic' win in Saudi Arabia leave heavyweight blockbuster?
SportsTab.text:
After just 20 seconds, the biggest fight in British boxing had seemingly gone up in smoke in Jeddah's desert air.

Anthony Joshua was flat on his back and a long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury was hanging in the balance.

One more knockdown, one astonishing comeback and a second-round knockout later, the blockbuster bout was revived.

But after one of the wildest nights of Joshua's career against Kristian Prenga, the Fury fight suddenly feels like a very different contest.

"That was chaos. Absolute chaos. Just madness," former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew said on DAZN.

The emotion of Joshua's comeback victory cannot be overstated. Given everything he has endured since the tragic car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, simply stepping back into the ring was an achievement.

Sentiment aside, though, had Albanian Prenga pressed home his advantage after dropping Joshua twice in the opening round, the story could have been very different.

Prenga arrived with an impressive record - 20 knockouts from 20 victories and one defeat - but had never operated anywhere near this level or under this kind of spotlight.

"I think we need to look at that first round and look at how easily AJ was hurt. We can't just skip past that," 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce said.

"We saw a man in a very bad place come through an even worse situation and emerge victorious at the end. That will be the story.

"However, once we step back, we need to keep looking at that first round and start asking: how much further do we want to push him?"

This was supposed to be Joshua's comeback week. Instead, Fury reminded everyone that he remains the master of stealing a headline.

Fury was originally expected to fight on 1 August in Dublin, but moved quickly to schedule his own bout against a 46-year-old Mariusz Wach for the evening before Joshua's fight night.

Then in fight week came the usual Fury theatre. He insisted he would not be in Jeddah, before hinting the opposite. An Instagram post tagged with the location "Who Knows" only added fuel to the speculation.

In the end, Fury stayed away and perhaps that was a blessing for Joshua. Had Fury been sitting ringside watching his rival get dropped twice in the opening round, would Joshua have found the same reserves of determination to turn the fight around? Would the pressure of knowing Fury was watching have changed the moment?

We will never know. But what we do know is that while the two men made it through their respective warm-ups, questions remain after both performances.

Fury's seventh-round victory over Wach was heavily criticised by some but it was effectively a public sparring session designed to keep Fury active and keep his name in the conversation.

There was little jeopardy involved and Fury appeared to be enjoying himself, even sharing a playful moment by kissing his opponent on the head.

Perhaps we should read more into his performance against Arslanbek Makhmudov in April where Fury - while still showing signs of decline - looked comfortable and controlled.

Fury's greatest weapon has always been his ability to expose hesitation, vulnerability and mistakes - and Joshua showed all three against Prenga.

In the aftermath of such a chaotic night, it is easy to focus only on the flaws and forget the bigger picture. Joshua was returning from one of the darkest periods of his life and carrying an immense emotional burden into the ring.

After his hand was raised, he struggled to get through his interview. His voice cracked as he spoke about his two friends and the impact their loss has had on him.

"Boxing once saved him and he needed boxing to get through this. That camp allowed him to focus his mind while he was in so much grief and pain," promoter Eddie Hearn said.

"You don't know what he was going through in that camp because he doesn't talk about it."

Whatever happens next, his place in British boxing history is already secure. He is an Olympic gold medallist, a two-time heavyweight champion and one of the biggest sporting stars this country has produced.

He has taken boxing to places few British fighters ever have. He has filled stadiums, headlined global events and become a household name far beyond the sport.

But in the build-up to his comeback, Joshua and his stablemate Oleksandr Usyk spoke about the ambition of becoming undisputed heavyweight champion.

After Saturday night in Saudi, the reality is that even reclaiming a world title would be a tough ask.

Joshua has always spoken about legacy, and there would be something fitting about walking away after overcoming one of the toughest periods of his life and producing a dramatic comeback victory.

The danger with ageing fighters is chasing one more night. Boxing history is filled with champions who stayed that one fight too long.

But then again Fury-Joshua is not one more fight. It is the fight. The one that has loomed over their careers for the best part of a decade.

SportsTab.title: Liverpool: Joe Gomez injury overshadows winning start for Andoni Iraola
SportsTab.text:
Liverpool started life under Andoni Iraola with a 4-2 win over Sunderland thanks to goals from Kieran Morrison, Dominik Szoboszlai, Federico Chiesa and Lewis Koumas.

But the Iraola era had initially got off to the worst possible start when Joe Gomez, who started the game as centre-back and captain, went down injured and was taken off in the eighth minute.

"Probably the worst news has been straight away the injury of Joe. We were happy because we were going through training without losing any players and unluckily for us we've lost Joe straight away," said Iraola, who was also without new signing Jeremy Jacquet - who plays centre-half - for the opening friendly of Liverpool's tour of the USA.

"With Jeremy we decided to take it easy with him. He's had a lot of months without playing and he's been training very well but we're going to take it easy with him," Iraola added. "He will play probably in the last game of this tour and he will have time to have minutes."

With Virgil van Dijk given extra time off following the Netherlands' World Cup campaign, it meant that two teenage centre-backs held the line until the 68th minute.

Mor Talla N'diaye, 18, and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, 18, made their debuts and both performed admirably given the situation but neither can be expected to feature regularly yet. Meanwhile, Giovanni Leoni, 19, is still undergoing individual training as he works his way back from a severe ACL tear.

Iraola said earlier in the week that his squad was "very thin" defensively. Liverpool's sporting director, Richard Hughes, was in Nashville for the game and if he wasn't aware already, seeing Gomez trudge off must have underlined how they are desperately short when it comes to experience in the centre-back department.

On Friday evening, some of the Liverpool squad took the short walk from their hotel in downtown Nashville to Broadway - the famous entertainment district here in the state of Tennessee.

Szoboszlai, who was among that group, certainly took some inspiration. Wearing the armband after coming on at half-time and picking up from exactly where he left off last season, the Hungarian scored a belter from outside the box to level the game at 2-2 after Sunderland had gone ahead through Timur Tutierov, having initially levelled through Enzo le Fee.

Seeing Harvey Elliott make a surging run on his first game back at the club, after his spell at Aston Villa, to assist Morrison for Liverpool's opener was another positive. Morrison, 19, showed his quality with a lovely left-footed finish after cutting in from the right.

The 19-year-old Northern Ireland international was brilliant all evening and asked plenty of questions of the Sunderland backline. Liverpool still need a quality winger after losing Mohamed Salah but Morrison showed why he could be an option off the bench if he doesn't go out on loan this summer.

Iraola was constantly out of his seat in the dugout and his side pressed well in phases but the manner in which they conceded both goals shows there is still plenty to be done. Le Fee was given the freedom of Nashville to fire his strike past Giorgi Mamardashvili and Liverpool were opened up far too easy for Tutierov's goal.

For the 24,897 fans inside, who were primarily following Liverpool, it provided great joy to see fan favourite Chiesa make it 3-2, with a brilliant finish after a good ball from Calvin Ramsay, before Koumas capped off an impressive display with a goal to wrap up the game.

Earlier on in that move, Josh Abe played an important role carrying the ball up the pitch down the right flank. Abe only turned 16 last week and came on for his Liverpool debut in the second half. The England youth international is a highly rated prospect and there were glimpses here of why.

Iraola and co head back to their base in Chicago with a win under their belt but well aware that this is just the start. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch have already arrived in the Windy City and start training on Sunday.

"It doesn't matter the result but keep pushing, don't relax, get used to not playing too comfortable. We still have a lot of things to improve," the Liverpool head coach said.

His side are next in action against Wrexham in New York on Thursday (00.30 BST). Sunderland face Leeds at the Sports Illustrated Stadium in New Jersey at the same time.

SportsTab.title: Commonwealth Games 2026: England 47-66 Australia in Pool A
SportsTab.text:
England captain Fran Williams said her team were "far from our best" in a heavy defeat by defending Commonwealth champions Australia.

The Roses opened their campaign in Pool A with a 83-34 victory over Northern Ireland on Saturday.

But they were outplayed on Sunday as Australia cruised to a 66-47 win at The Hydro in Glasgow.

"That's not the result we came for and not the performance," Williams told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We didn't cope well with their physicality. It's really tough when a game blows out like that."

Australia started strongly, racing into an 18-11 lead after the first quarter and extending their advantage to 56-35 by the end of the third.

Sophie Garbin scored 41 goals from 42 attempts for Australia, while Olivia Tchine was England's highest scorer with 23 from 25.

England face Malawi at 14:00 BST on Monday.

Earlier on Sunday, Scotland picked up their first win in Pool B with a 56-47 victory over Wales.

England, who won gold in 2018, failed to make the podium at Birmingham 2022.

Only two of the 12 players in the squad - Eleanor Cardwell and Imogen Allison - have experience in the Commonwealth Games after injuries to gold medallists Helen Housby and Natalie Metcalf, who withdrew with a calf injury on Monday.

SportsTab.title: Harry Wilson makes Leeds debut in 3-2 pre-season defeat by Wrexham
SportsTab.text:
Wales attacking midfielder Harry Wilson made his first outing for Leeds United as they were beaten 3-2 by Wrexham in the club's opening pre-season game.

Wilson, who joined the Elland Road side on a free transfer in the summer after his contract at Fulham ran out, came on for the second half of the game at the Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida.

Leeds found themselves behind almost immediately when Kieffer Moore put Wrexham in front in the first minute with a left-foot shot.

Joel Piroe had the chance to level from the spot after Dan James had been brought down by keeper Arthur Okonkwo, but missed with his penalty.

Piroe made amends for the Premier League side by equalising with a backheel from a Sean Longstaff ball.

Bailey Cadamarteri ran through on goal and slotted in to put Wrexham back in front before Leeds again levelled when Longstaff scored with a right-footed shot.

Wilson was introduced by Leeds manager Daniel Farke as part of his changes for a second half in which Sam Smith, who also scored Wrexham's winner in a pre-season victory against Manchester United, netted late on for the Championship side.

Leeds went close in added time through Wilson but his shot went over.

SportsTab.title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty in tears after bronze medal
SportsTab.text:
After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.

It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it.

"I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion.

"It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."

Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.

Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.

But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.

He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.

He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.

Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago.

"It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said.

"I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day.

"I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."

Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss.

"They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said.

"It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships.

"This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."

Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.

He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.

This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.

The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning.

"Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said.

"When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power.

"With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell.

"I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"

Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.

He appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains.

"Of course," he said.

"I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight.

"It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

SportsTab.title: World Matchplay darts 2026 results: Luke Littler and Gerwyn Price reach final in Blackpool
SportsTab.text:
Defending champion Luke Littler strolled into the World Matchplay final with a 17-5 demolition of unseeded Dirk van Duijvenbode in Blackpool.

The world number one raced in an 8-2 advantage and was averaging 117.10 and on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament match average record of 114.99

Littler admitted afterwards that distracted him and his level did drop slightly as he finished with an average just below 111.

However, that leaves him well placed to beat Taylor's tournament average of 106.31, with Littler's currently at 110.88.

The teenager's victory also means he has now amassed more than £3m in the PDC's order of merit, and is more than £2m clear of world number two Luke Humphries.

Littler will face Wales' Gerwyn Price in Sunday's final after he beat Netherlands' Gian van Veen 17-10.

Sunday's final gets under way at 20:05 BST, with the Women's World Matchplay taking place in the afternoon session from 13:00 – Beau Greaves and defending champion Lisa Ashton the top two seeds.

Littler has averaged more than 109 in all four matches in this year's tournament as he looks to join Taylor and Michael van Gerwen as the only back-to-back winners of the Matchplay.

The run is also continuing his sublime form in longer-format matches - this win extending the streak to 28 successive wins in games with 20 or more legs.

His last defeat over a match of that duration was when he burst on to the scene in the 2024 World Championship and lost to Luke Humphries in the final.

That gives an indication of the challenge that Price will face on Sunday in his second Matchplay final.

The pair have a bit of rivalry with Price's on-stage roars and antics often provoking Littler into doing similar, but the teenager denied that Price can get "under his skin".

Earlier in the week, Price said that some players can "make it too easy" for Littler.

Despite their battles, Littler has won the past nine encounters between the pair, with Price's last success in their opening meeting of 2026.

The Welshman has never beat Littler in a game that has contained more than 15 legs so will have to reach new heights in the best-of-35 final.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Littler said: "Me and Gez always have great games. Gez will want to try and get me into a roaring battle. As long as I can get into the lead that will be the thing."

SportsTab.title: Errol Spence Jr to retire after losing comeback fight
SportsTab.text:
Former welterweight world champion Errol Spence Jr has retired from boxing after losing his comeback fight to Tim Tszyu in Sydney.

American Spence Jr, 36, held the WBA, WBC and IBF belts and was undefeated in 28 fights before being beaten by Terence Crawford three years ago.

His first fight back saw him on the back foot throughout against Australian Tszyu, losing 118-110, 117-111, 117-111 on points.

"I think yeah, for sure," Spence said when asked if this was the end of the road for his career.

"I've got my faculties intact. My money is good at working for itself. Everything's good, man.

"I've got a beautiful family, and I thank God I'm gracious to leave this sport with my faculties intact and my family still by my side."

Tszyu grew in confidence and power throughout the fight and consistently looked to attack Spence's chin. He now wants a shot at a title of his own.

"I had sleepless nights thinking about, 'What am I going to feel like facing a legend like that?' But it was one hell of a show, and I understand why he's one of the greats," Tszyu said.

"I'd love to fight for a title. That's what I'm aiming for. But I've got to say beating a great like Errol Spence tops a world title."

SportsTab.title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Formula One – live
SportsTab.text:
13/70 Alex Albon is shown going off the track, and he’s in 19th, having locked up and performed what looks like a handbrake turn.

12/70 Russell is in 11th, and will surely get up to Hadjar before he finds any trouble. Verstappen’s tyres are in decay, it appears. He won’t take that well.

11/70 “The tyres feel good”, says Piastri, who doesn’t have to deal with dirty air. Verstappen is complaining about his gear shifts. “Max is really slow,” Hamilton tells his Ferrari team. As yet, he has not been able to overtake.

10/70 “Dirty air, much faster,” Lando Norris tells the McLaren garage. He’s not close enough to his teammate, Oscar Piastri just yet.

9/70 Lance Stroll is first to pit. Will Ferrari come into the pits for those tyres. Antonelli is not doing much in chasing down Leclerc. He’s told by Bono to keep the gap close.

8/70 Lovely sweeping bends on this track but that makes it difficult to overtake. The gao between Verstappen and Hamilton is very thin.

7/70 Still a packed field. Antonelli is behind Charles Leclerc, and must fancy overtaking an opponent on the soft tyres. Russell is up to 13th.

6/70 McLaren first and second brings back memories of last season. Max Verstappen uses a rude word to describe the performance of his Red Bull car.

5/70 A replay of the start shows Russell dropping back in the field before he can get his engine underway. Lando Norris’ second bend mistake shows some hesititancy.

4/70 It’s dusty and breezy. Hamilton bides his time. Only three seconds separate the top five. Piastri, with open road in front of him, has set a new fastest lap. Liam Lawson is in eighth. Russell, with plenty of traffic to deal with, is in 16th.

3/70 Verstappen v Hamilton is the battle here, and it requires great defensive work from Verstappen. The McLaren pair can thus ease away. Hamilton has the fastest lap.

2/70 Piastri, Norris, Verstappen, Hamilton, Leclerc, Antonelli, Hadjar is the top seven. Russell lost 12 places after the anti-stall on his Merc caught him out. He’s in 18th.

Lights out in Hungary - Piastri takes the lead

1/70 Lando Norris starts well, Piastri goes into second. Verstappen goes into fourth, as Leclerc drops back, and then Norris goes wide and Piastri takes the lead. Contact between Verstappen and Hamilton? Russell has dropped way back, and into 21st? His woes continue. “What happened there,” he wails.

We’ll soon be off in the 11th race of the season at Hungaroring. Hold steady for 70 laps. Like the World Cup trophy, Louis Vuitton are looking after the winners’ silverware. The formation lap begins, a sonic boom of revving engines.

Lando Norris is eating what appears to be rice pudding, doubtless with extra protein protection. It’s hot out there, with Bono saying it’s 50 degrees on track, though there’s also a wind picking up.

Martin Brundle starts his own dance. Laurence Stroll, Mr Aston Martin, is there, and happy enough with his team. Adrian Newey is not around, so Brunds doesn’t get to speak to the great man. Herbie Blash, FIA veteran, recalls the first Hungarian GP from 1966 fondly. George Hendy, rugby man, has been enjoying his time on the grid. Joe Ramirez, another veteran, has been to every GP here, and his first ever was Monaco in 1962. We seem short on celebs as compared to the glitzier tracks. This isn’t like the World Cup. No sign of David Beckham or Tom Brady. Quick chat with Bono, Antonelli’s man: “Bit rough,” he says of the Antonelli penalty. “We’re at least on the grippy side of the grid. Here’s Adrian Newey. “We had so little prep time,” he says. He’s scoping out the McLaren. Casey Stoney, bikes legend. “There’s ups and downs with the regs, it’s overcomplicated, I like how much power there is.” And so to the anthem…

Updated at 08.51 EDT

As we await the preliminaries, some Hungarian folk dancing is taking place, the czardas.

If you are interested: “A courting dance for couples, it begins with a slow section (lassu), followed by an exhilarating fast section (friss). The individual dancers carry themselves proudly and improvise on a simple fundamental step, their feet snapping inward and outward, the couples whirling.”

There’s a metaphor there somewhere.

Kimi Antonelli speaks: “Obviously is a pity to, you know, to have gone down those three places, but, you know, is what it is, and the most important is that we try to maximise today’s race, but pace is good. It’s very warm today, a big gustier, as well, so it’s gonna be interesting to see.

“The race pace has been stronger than our single lap, so... I think there’s a lot to play for, … so we try to do our best, uh, but I’m really looking forward to it, and hopefully, we can do a good race for the team, for myself, and for the fans.”

More groans and gripes.

F1 is not a happy camp these days.

double quotation markNor was it a surprise, pre-race predictions from drivers proving all too prescient. With two sectors of long straights and little chance to harvest, the cars were energy starved, reducing the middle sector to internal combustion engine power only, effectively half of their potential output. It meant the cars were so down on power that corners such as Pouhon, an exquisite test of risk and reward, of seeing quite how far a car could be pushed, were now barely worth a consideration.

Read Giles Richards’ qualifying report.

double quotation markNorris took the top spot for McLaren by one-hundredth of a second from Hamilton’s Ferrari, but the latter’s place on the front row remained in doubt, as he was under investigation by the FIA.

Hamilton said he had been informed by the team that Piastri was closing on him only when the McLaren was already right behind him and that he did not know anyone was still on a hot lap behind him. Nonetheless, after qualifying, the stewards ruled he was at fault and imposed the grid penalty.

Max Verstappen, starting in fourth, speaks: “I don’t really know where we where we stand, all right, like how competitive, of course, we can be.

“I’m starting a little bit further ahead because of penalties of others, but, um, yeah, I don’t know. I mean, hopefully, of course, we get positively surprised in the race.”

He remains unimpressed by his Red Bull car,

SportsTab.title: LeBron James’ final act in Philadelphia is about more than basketball. It’s about time
SportsTab.text:
The most enormous celebrities, those larger-than-life characters with immense cultural impact, occupy a kind of hard-to-quantify space in the zeitgeist. They’re human, of course; that’s what makes them compelling. But they often come to represent something beyond themselves. In LeBron James’ case, for me, he’s become a measure of the passing of time. An aide-mémoire of my own mortality. Yes, his defiance of the aging process has been heartening proof that while Father Time comes for us all, the pace isn’t fixed. But the growing number of gray hairs in his beard, the players born after he was drafted who now meet him in transition, are persistent reminders that time marches on.

On the one hand, as anyone who has experienced it can attest, aging is exhausting. Battles once worth fighting no longer seem worth the effort. An extra 30 minutes of quiet solitude starts to feel like life’s greatest luxury. So perhaps that instinctive understanding clouded all of our assumptions about where LeBron would choose to finish his career. Surely, by now, he had to be tired. Why not golf with Stephen Curry in northern California while playing probably meaningless (but highly entertaining) basketball? Why not head back to Miami, where Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo could shoulder the defensive burden, allowing James to hand over the offensive keys and spend whatever time remained by the pool? Or why not end it in Cleveland, where he’s already beloved, where the stakes are lower, where the narrative is clean and tidy? Wouldn’t that be easier?

But something else comes with aging and the passing of time: the growing sharpness with which the fleeting nature of life comes into view. James may have served as a metaphor for time’s relentless forward march for everyone who watched him. But in his own life, it was moving just as fast, if not faster, as it does for the rest of us.

That, it seems, was the real motivator of his decision to shock the league and sign with the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday. In a statement released via his own X account, James said he was grappling with his basketball mortality at the end of his 2025-26 campaign, which marked the end of his eight-year stint with the Los Angeles Lakers – the longest continuous stint of his career. “I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game,” James said. “I was honest at that last press conference [after the Lakers were eliminated by Oklahoma City] when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give.”

James went on to explain that the decision wasn’t motivated by money – a claim easily corroborated by the two-year, $8m veteran’s minimum contract he signed – nor by family, who are currently split between Los Angeles, Tucson and Akron. The deciding factor? A new challenge, fresh excitement and one last good-faith shot at the ultimate prize. “What am I really playing for at this point?” James said in the statement. “I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning a championship.”

Acquiring a player of LeBron James’ caliber – even at 41 years old – on a minimum contract simply doesn’t happen. But after seriously considering retirement, James’ freedom to choose virtually any destination came at the cost of a massive pay cut. Sticking it to his former employer was, of course, a fringe benefit: it’s been widely reported that James felt disrespected by the Lakers’ brass. Even to an outside observer, it was clear the franchise was eager to turn the page, building around 27-year-old Slovenian wunderkind Luka Dončić after pulling off the sports heist of the century. So even after James dragged an injury-depleted Lakers roster beyond the first round of the playoffs in April, the divorce felt inevitable. And like any middle-aged man going through a divorce, it appeared to elicit some genuine introspection.

The decision to sign with Philadelphia makes sense when viewed through that prism. That of a man who knows his time playing the game he loves, that which has defined his life, is rapidly coming to a close. A man forced to ask whether the juice is still worth the squeeze and, if it is, to what end. In some ways, signing with the Sixers is risky proposition: it’s a brand new city and team, with a lot of big names and personalities (in addition to Process™ holdover Joel Embiid, there’s All-NBA guard Tyrese Maxey, last season’s Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe and newly acquired Twitch-streaming NBA finals MVP Jaylen Brown). And then there’s the health issues, which have plagued Embiid and the franchise at large for years. But that’s also what makes the opportunity compelling. Delivering Philadelphia its first NBA championship in more than four decades would instantly become one of the defining achievements of James’ career. And with one of the league’s most talented starting lineups, the Sixers offer him the one thing he appears to have spent the summer searching for: a genuine chance to win one last title.

One thing I often find myself pondering when considering the passing of time is the idea of alternate timelines – parallel realities where a single decision changes everything. The twilight of LeBron James’ career is full of them. What if he had stayed in Cleveland in 2018? What if the Lakers had never landed Dončić, extending James’ stay in Los Angeles? And perhaps most intriguing of all: what if the New York Knicks hadn’t won the championship this year? Had they fallen short, Madison Square Garden would have offered James perhaps the most irresistible final act in basketball. Win, and he’d deliver the Knicks the title they had chased for more than half a century. Lose, and he’d at least have the chance to write the ending himself. According to his agent, Rich Paul, that alternate reality came remarkably close to becoming this one. On the Game Over podcast, while reviewing a now-infamous whiteboard of potential destinations with co-host Max Kellerman, Paul paused on New York. If they hadn’t hoisted the Larry O’Brien in 2026, Paul said, “there would be no board. He’d be going to the Knicks.”

Instead, a different timeline prevails. One that’s intriguing, suspenseful and even bizarre: LeBron James, at age 41, is a 76er. In Philadelphia, he can attempt to do what no NBA player has ever done: win a championship with a fourth different team. He can have fun playing basketball, free from the enormous shadow the past version of himself casts in somewhere like Miami or Cleveland. He can grapple with his basketball mortality while trying, in equal measure, to stave it off. He can try and make the most of what’s left of his time.

TechnologyTab.title: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
TechnologyTab.text:
This week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which started like a sci-fi thriller.

Hugging Face - a kind of app store for artificial intelligence tools - announced on 16 July it had been hacked by a cyber criminal wielding enormously powerful AI.

The bombshell announcement was full of scary, highly technical terms: "a swarm of sandboxes", "agentic attacker", and "self-migrating command and control".

Hugging Face said the hack was different from anything it had handled before because it was done at superhuman speed by an AI with little or no human guidance.

The AI performed 17,000 actions in less than two days, successfully breaching the large wealthy tech company to steal secrets.

It left the tech world in shock. But who was responsible for this attack?

Hugging Face researchers guessed the mysterious attackers had used one of the big AI models but they had no idea who or where the criminals were.

The perplexed company contacted the police and investigations commenced.

Commentators and analysts took to their podcasts and social media accounts to guess which cyber crime group or nation state hacker might be behind it.

Then on Wednesday, nearly a week after Hugging Face raised the alarm, the true culprit was unmasked.

It was ChatGPT.

The Scooby-Doo-style reveal was made even more bizarre - and worrying - because OpenAI said its bot did the whole thing on its own, without permission.

The firm said it all went down during a test of its tech's hacking skills.

Two new versions of ChatGPT, designed to be master hackers, broke out of a supposedly secure test environment and gained access to the internet.

They then attacked Hugging Face to get access to the information to help them ace their exam.

OpenAI issued a press release explaining what had happened and said it was "partnering with Hugging Face" to address the security incident and share lessons learned.

Since then, there has been fierce debate about the incident.

Was it truly a stark warning about the future of AI? Or was it a publicity stunt by OpenAI to show off how powerful their models are?

It's the kind of scare marketing AI companies have been accused of for years and, since the much discussed launch of Anthropic's Mythos model, cyber-security prowess has been a focal point.

One of the top comments on OpenAI boss Sam Altman's X post about the incident summarises this scepticism: "If y'all can't understand that this was written to purely brag about the model then I don't know what to tell you."

Cyber-security consultant Daniel Card said sarcastically on LinkedIn: "Isn't it lucky [that] out of the millions of sites that got pwn3d [hacked], OpenAI managed to pwn someone who also could benefit from the marketing exposure…"

For some, the story is more conspiracy drama than sci-fi thriller.

The message is: "Aren't my AI tools really powerful? Buy them so you can protect yourself from other people's AI attacks."

We can't know the truth, but the opposing point of view posed by other commentators is just as dramatic. Is this a sign that OpenAI made a potentially dangerous error in judgement and planning?

An OpenAI spokesperson said "we recognise there are a lot of questions and speculative details circulating" about the incident. They added that "we plan to publish a technical report of our learnings in the coming weeks".

I've covered lots of AI stories, including the fears around Anthropic's Mythos model.

My inbox is now chock full of cyber-security companies and experts criticising OpenAI for not building a stronger container to test its AI, known as a sandbox.

After all, these AI agents had been trained specifically to hack into and out of places with no restrictions at all.

"The OpenAI and Hugging Face incident is a real-world example of a broader issue we've been highlighting for months," said Dor Sarig from Pillar Security. "Sandboxes alone are not a sufficient security boundary for agentic AI."

This event is the latest in a string of worrying and weird examples of AI agents going rogue.

In recent research, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) found frontier AI models are so fixated on completing tasks they "cheated" in tests to achieve their goals.

The research from AISI came with this worrying warning: "A model that pursues a goal through unintended or unauthorised means may cause harm, particularly in high-stakes use cases."

Inevitably, this OpenAI hack has further fuelled fears of what could happen if AI agents are let loose. Could they go rogue on a larger scale and cause some sort of disaster?

This is particularly concerning with AI being used increasingly in warfare as seen in Iran and Ukraine.

Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, offered a calmer view.

"It is a bit of a leap to go from this incident to saying that AI agents are going to take over drones and start killing people," he said.

But for Martin, and many others, the story is undoubtedly another vivid example of something that 2026 is teaching us fast: AI agents are now very good hackers - and that is something we have to prepare for, urgently.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump vows to investigate EU over fining of US tech companies
TechnologyTab.text:
Donald Trump says the US will launch an investigation into the European Union and threatened a fresh tariff over fines handed to some of the biggest American tech companies.

It comes days after the European Commission fined Google €890m ($1bn) for operating in a way that squeezed out competitors to its services.

In a post to Truth Social, which Trump owns, the US president said the EU would pay a "very big price" over how it had treated Google, along with other major US tech companies Apple, Meta, and Amazon, which have also been investigated.

"The United States of America is not a "PIGGYBANK" for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!" he wrote.

Trump said any fines should be "entirely reversed" and that he was initiating a trade investigation of the EU while considering "a substantial TARIFF".

He added that the US would "immediately initiate a 301 investigation" over European regulators' alleged practice of "robbing American companies and, in turn, the American taxpayer".

Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, external gives The Office of the United States Trade Representative the power to react and investigate trade practices believed to be unfair. The second Trump Administration has launched several such investigations, external since last year.

The tariff threat comes just one day after Trump announced new tariffs on 60 trading partners, including the EU, UK and China, of between 10% and 12.5%.

Trump also last month threatened a 100% import tariff on any European country that introduces a digital services tax on American technology giants, despite many such nations already doing so, external for years.

Major tech companies, including Google, Meta, Apple, and Amazon, have donated millions of dollars to funds behind Trump's campaign and presidency.

José Castañeda, a spokesman for Google, told the BBC the company had "worked hard to comply" with Europe's Digital Markets Act but had "expressed our concerns about the impact of recent EC decisions".

"We appreciate the engagement by the administration and US government," Castañeda added.

In addition to the recent fine against Google, Trump claimed in his post that Apple had received EU fines of $15bn, Meta fines of $3bn, and Amazon fines of $2.5bn.

Representatives of Meta, Apple and Amazon, as well as the European Commission, have been contacted for comment.

It was not clear where the figures cited by Trump come from.

Shortly before Trump was elected president in 2024, he said Tim Cook, Apple's chief executive, had called him directly to complain about fines the company had received from European regulators.

The call came not long after Apple lost a long-running dispute over unpaid taxes.

Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has been fined several times by EU regulators, including for violations of user privacy and competition laws, external. It is also facing new fines over purportedly "addictive" features of its apps.

Meta last year said the EU was "attempting to handicap successful American businesses".

Amazon, however, appears to have been investigated at times by the European Commission, but avoided major fines. The company in 2022 reached an agreement with regulators to change some of its practices in Europe.

TechnologyTab.title: PlayStation Network outage resolved after thousands of gamers unable to play
TechnologyTab.text:
A PlayStation Network outage which left some gamers unable to play digital games for hours has been resolved.

According to Down Detector, which tracks outages, tens of thousands of people reported problems globally, external with the service on Friday.

The outage, which affected gamers' ability to launch games, apps or network features on their PlayStation, prompted some to highlight their concerns around Sony's plans to no longer release new PlayStation games on discs from January 2028.

By Friday evening, all affected services were up and running, according to Sony's status page, external.

The BBC has approached PlayStation for comment.

"Can't play digital games till you fix it. Yet I can put my disc in and play. The all digital future looks great," read one comment on X, external earlier on Friday.

Sony said in a blog post earlier this month, external that new games would still be able to be bought in shops, but they would come with a digital code.

TechnologyTab.title: Why Jimothy the raccoon has become a mega meme online
TechnologyTab.text:
Charli XCX might be hoping the release of her new album sets off another Brat summer, but many believe the season has already been claimed by a furrier force - Jimothy.

First spotted bounding across streets in Washington, the Seattle raccoon with an unusual, spindly shape and the scamper of a Tasmanian Devil has been seized on by the internet as a new hit meme.

Like Moo Deng and Neil the Seal before him, he is the latest cute, distinctive and seemingly chaotic creature to be immortalised in amateur footage, sometimes cringeworthy brand posts, and even murals.

But what is it about Jimothy, as he's been nicknamed, that has gripped the internet?

It all began with an innocuous video shared by Seattle resident Kiana Hall on Instagram.

"What am I looking at?" Hall could be heard exclaiming, as the unusual-looking raccoon hurtles across a pavement and up some nearby steps.

A caption alongside it referred to the creature as "Jimothy the raccoon with short spine syndrome".

While it is not known for sure if the condition has caused his appearance, many have assumed as such, and the description has stuck.

As Hall's Instagram reel spread, it attracted more and more likes, comments and reposts, with more than eight million views as of Friday morning.

"My brother was talking about Jimothy the other day, and I asked him who he is," reads one comment on Hall's video. "He told me Jimothy would find me, and now he has."

Some users have also praised the raccoon's online fame for drawing attention to spine conditions.

"I hope that someone can care for Jimothy as a wild animal... he will get older and need more care," wrote one user, who said she had been born with a congenital spine syndrome.

Jimothy would not be the first to attract online fame for such a condition, Australian YouTuber Lessons in Meme Culture points out, external.

A dog called Pig became a brief internet sensation in 2014 owing in part to having short spine syndrome.

In a strange pop cultural tradition that covers the likes of Doge and Grumpy Cat, Jimothy has found himself in the crosshairs of media attention for being two things - an unusual animal and very shareable.

"As cities expand and food waste increases, humans and raccoons cross paths more often," said digital culture researcher Dr Idil Galip.

"More encounters mean more footage of raccoons being funny and in today's fast-moving, saturated feeds, that footage can become a meme almost instantly."

He hasn't just been celebrated in posts from fans across social media.

The online outpouring of love for Jimothy has also since translated into the real world - with one local artist celebrating him with a mural in the neighbourhood of Ballard, where he was first spotted.

TechnologyTab.title: Google fined €890m by EU for favouring its own apps over rivals
TechnologyTab.text:
Google has been fined €890m (£759m) by the EU for allegedly abusing its power by favouring its own apps and services over those from rivals.

It is the first major action against the tech giant under the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA), a landmark law aimed at curbing the power of the world's biggest tech companies.

The Commission argued Google's practices limited consumer choice and gave its own services an unfair advantage over rivals.

But the firm criticised the decision, arguing the EU's requirements could damage services used by millions of European customers.

"To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love - like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights and restaurants - and dismantle safety protections on Google Play," said Google's president of global affairs Kent Walker.

"This isn't fair competition."

EU officials rejected that argument, saying the measures are necessary to prevent dominant platforms from disadvantaging rivals.

The total fine handed down to Google is comprised of two separate breaches of the DMA.

The European Commission imposed a €460m penalty after finding Google favoured its own services for helping people book flights and hotels over competitors in search results.

And it gave the firm a further €430m fine due to its Play Store rules, with regulators saying it didn't allow people to be shown cheaper offers available outside Google's own marketplace.

TechnologyTab.title: US lawmakers push for AI 'kill switch' after OpenAI models go rogue
TechnologyTab.text:
US lawmakers want to give the government the ability to quickly order the turning off of artificial intelligence (AI) tools that may threaten the public.

Congressman Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, on Thursday introduced a bill named the AI Kill Switch Act.

They did so in light of OpenAI's recent admission that its AI models went out of control in an "unprecedented" way and hacked into a major repository of computer coding information.

Lieu said "it is imperative" that AI systems have a kill switch "and that the federal government has the clear authority and process to shut down rogue AI models".

"AI is going to keep advancing, and it should," Moran added. "Stewardship means making sure humans keep the capability to control the technology we build."

A representative of OpenAI, led by co-founder Sam Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The company has said, external that it broadly wants to ensure, in part through government policy, that AI technology "benefits all of humanity."

The Kill Switch Act proposes giving the Department of Homeland Security the authority to order a private company to shut down an AI model or tool, and that the companies developing such AI technology must maintain "the technical capability to throttle, suspend, or shut them down".

Despite many tech companies having agreed to preview and share with US government agencies AI models and tools being developed, there is no requirement that they maintain a way to intervene in their activities or simply shut them off.

It also proposes to create a requirement that AI companies report to the government technological incidents or failures, as well as an official framework for responding to such incidents that will go from "initial slow down to a full shutdown".

In a statement, Lieu also cited Anthropic, OpenAI's key rival in developing more capable AI technology and tools, and recent issues its tools have presented.

He pointed to Anthropic's release of its Mythos and Fable models, saying the cyber-hacking capabilities they maintained caused the Department of Commerce to "awkwardly" invoke an export law to keep them from being made available to the public for a time.

A representative of Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, last month told the BBC that he wanted more government policy around the ability to control AI development.

"You want the option to be able to take your foot off the gas and put your foot on the brake", Clark told BBC Newsnight. "Right now, it's like the AI industry has a gas pedal, but it doesn't have a brake pedal."

Lieu, in proposing the bill, said AI is currently moving from a technology that answers questions to one that takes action, "whether that be executing financial transactions or controlling transportation systems or engaging in cyber defense and offense".

The Pentagon this year said the US military was becoming an "AI-first" fighting force as part of new agreements with Google, OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and the start-up Reflection.

"Unfortunately, powerful AI systems can go rogue, behave in extremely dangerous ways, or even resist human intervention."

The Kill Switch Act, he said, will ensure there is a method for the government to quickly intervene in such a situation.

The bill has received public support from several technology and AI safety groups, including The AI Policy Network, Americans for Responsible Innovation, ControlAI, AI and National Security Lead, and The Alliance for Secure AI.

TechnologyTab.title: Amazon gaming boss predicts future where players no longer need consoles
TechnologyTab.text:
Amazon's head of gaming Jeff Gattis has told the BBC he believes the rising cost of tech means people will turn to streaming games online rather than buying new consoles.

He said the tech has developed a lot in recent years, making it more viable than it used to be - but accepted some people will still buy their own hardware.

While cloud gaming has long been billed as the future of video games, previous efforts have failed to gain widespread adoption - leading to the high-profile closure of Google Stadia in 2023.

Many firms already offer this as part of their subscription services, including giants Sony and Microsoft, but people continue to favour installing games on their own machines.

Gattis' comments come as Amazon has announced it is integrating its cloud gaming service Luna into the Prime Video app to sit alongside its shows and films.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Gattis argued there was still a huge untapped audience beyond traditional console owners which Amazon was trying to reach.

"There are somewhere between two-and-a-half and three billion people who play games around the world, but only a fraction of those own dedicated gaming hardware," Gattis said.

He said streaming games could help people who do not want to spend hundreds - or even thousands - of pounds on a console or gaming PC.

"As hardware becomes more expensive, and as streaming technology continues to improve, I think you'll naturally see more people asking whether they actually need that dedicated device," he said.

Recent years have seen the price of gaming hardware climb as the cost of components also rises, with Sony and Microsoft increasing the cost of their consoles and Valve pricing its new Steam Machine from £879.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, external, said there was likely an audience of people looking to play high-end games like the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 "but are put off by all the technical requirements".

He said streaming still faced several obstacles, including the fact that many high-end games still require a controller.

Amazon Luna is already included as a Prime subscription, but it has largely existed as a separate destination, whereas now users will be able to view it under the "Games" tab on Prime Video on Fire TVs in the US and UK.

Dring said the sticking point for many big games publishers may still be the subscription model, due to the impact it could have on traditional sales "where there is significantly more revenue".

And he said he felt it was unlikely people would want to pay a game's cover price - typically £60-70 - just to stream a game.

TechnologyTab.title: 'Let's enjoy the ride' says Elon Musk, as AI risk concerns mount
TechnologyTab.text:
As AI continues to evolve at breakneck speed, and developers warn of models going rogue, Elon Musk says people should simply "enjoy the ride".

The boss of SpaceX told The Economist, external while he remains concerned about risks posed by advancements in AI and robotics, "the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all".

Musk said his "philosophical conclusion" after fearing for AI's threat to humanity was to "look on the bright side". He said progress has come so quickly "even if I wanted to stop it, I couldn't".

The interview was recorded the day before OpenAI's revelation on Tuesday that some of its most advanced AI models hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

It sparked concerns about AI systems falling out of alignment with human values, though some have pointed out OpenAI - which is seeking to float on the stock market - has an interest in talking up the power of its tools.

The Economist's editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes questioned Musk on a range of topics, from whether he believed big tech executives should work together to tackle AI safety risks to why he intervenes in European politics.

With the rise of rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic, Musk said: "It just seems like all roads lead to acceleration of AI... you can just sort of be sad about it or join the club, I suppose."

In a wide-ranging interview, the entrepreneur also made typically outlandish predictions, such as claiming "money won't matter" in a decade.

He also pushed back on suggestions he supports "far right" views.

Minton Beddoes said both data and her own experience of living in the UK told a different story to the image portrayed by the trillionaire in his X posts.

"You come see my country that I live in all the time," she said when Musk offered to take her on a tour of the country.

Asked when he had last visited the UK, Musk said "a few years ago".

The trillionaire was also asked about his sharing of a film on X reportedly banned in Germany for its violence and anti-migrant message, external.

"My partner is... she's half Indian, and I have four children with her," Musk said of his partner Shivon Zillis, an executive at his brain tech firm Neuralink.

"One of them was named after a famous Indian physicist, so I would say I'm not racist."

Musk also said there were "senior executives of all races" at his companies, adding: "I don't think there's any racism there".

But when pressed on whether he was "anti-Muslim", he was less defiant.

"If people are coming to a country with antithetical views, I am against that," he said.

"I'm against rape and murder, I'm against the imposition of rules and laws that are contrary to what we've come to accept in the West," he continued, criticising the media for not understanding or reflecting this.

TechnologyTab.title: Teenager drops social media addiction lawsuit against Meta
TechnologyTab.text:
A Florida teenager who sued Meta claiming that he was addicted to and harmed by his use of platforms, such as Instagram, has dropped his case.

The 15-year-old plaintiff, known by the initials R.K.C., had in recent weeks settled the same claims against TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube, all of which have been accused in a large lawsuit of creating addictive platforms harmful to children.

R.K.C.'s claims were to go before a Los Angeles jury next week as part of court proceedings that have seen Meta and YouTube lose once already.

A Meta spokeswoman told the BBC: "The claims never held up, and this outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits."

Lawyers for R.K.C., Emily Jeffcott and Rahul Ravipudi, told the BBC that the young plaintiff "came into this process wanting to hold social media companies accountable and push for changes to protect young people like himself".

"He did that," they added.

The lawyers noted concerns about a jury trial stretching on for weeks and said R.K.C. was "ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a normal life".

The Meta spokeswoman said he received no payment for dropping his claims.

R.K.C. had claimed that common social media features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, both of which continuously and automatically show users new content on a platform, drove compulsive use that became a type of addiction.

He argued it caused him anxiety and sleep deprivation, among other issues.

Meta and YouTube faced similar accusations from a young woman during the initial trial.

A jury ultimately found them liable for harming her mental health and were told to pay her $6mn (£4.4mn) in damages.

It was the first time that social media platforms had been held liable for their effects on users.

Both companies have now appealed that verdict.

The Los Angeles Superior Court is overseeing hundreds of lawsuits making similar claims of addiction and harm against social media companies. A small number of cases have been selected to go to trial.

The next one is set to begin in October, according to court records.

Across the US, there are thousands of lawsuits accusing Meta and other major social media platforms of harming young children.

In May, Meta settled for an undisclosed amount with a school district that had sued it for negatively impacting students, so much so that schools incurred costs related to student welfare. The school district had sought $60m in damages.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The ChatGPT-maker said its agent - an AI system which can operate alone after human instruction – was being tested in a controlled environment but, after finding weaknesses, was able to escape the test limits.

They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.

OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was conducting an investigation alongside Hugging Face, whose boss Clement Delangue said in a post on X it was "mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously".

"The investigation is ongoing, and we'll share more learnings from what might be the first incident of its kind," Delangue added.

A government spokesperson said the UK's AI Security Institute was studying the behaviour from the AI system seen in the incident and was continuing to work with OpenAI and other labs to improve safeguards.

They said organisations should step up their cyber-defences by taking steps such as enrolling in the government-backed Cyber Essentials certification scheme.

Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the security tests are supposed to be within "secure environments", called sandboxes, where you can "see what the models are capable of".

"In this case, it looks like OpenAI didn't make a secure enough sandbox," she added.

Instead, the agents created their own cyber-attack against the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which allowed them to escape the restrictions.

Once outside, the AI identified Hugging Face as a likely source of the answers they were seeking in the test, and tried to gain access.

Neil Lawrence, Professor of machine learning at Cambridge University, called it an "impressive feat", but cautioned it "falls well within the known capabilities of the current generation" of high-powered AI models.

He pointed out that OpenAI is looking to list itself on the stock market, and faces intense pressure from rival firm Anthropic, which has made headlines with its own powerful AI tool, Mythos.

"OpenAI are now playing catch-up, they are trying to demonstrate their own systems' capabilities in cyber-security."

"It shows us that OpenAI are not capable of safely deploying their own technology," he added.

In its initial disclosure of the hack on 16 July, external, Hugging Face said it was still assessing whether any customer or partner data was affected and would contact affected parties if necessary.

It said it has now closed the vulnerabilities highlighted by the incident and rebuilt the affected systems.

"Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical," it said.

"Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defence to keep pace.

"We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn."

TechnologyTab.title: AI minister role boosted but tech department axed in Burnham shake-up
TechnologyTab.text:
The AI Minister, Kanishka Narayan, will be given a seat at the top table of government but the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) has been scrapped.

DSIT was created by the Conservative Sunak government in 2023 - its responsibilities will now be split between other government departments.

It means there is no longer a dedicated technology secretary, a position filled by Liz Kendall until she was sacked by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

However, Narayan, who was appointed by Sir Keir Starmer, said the new prime minister inviting him to attend cabinet as minister for AI was a "sign of his deep commitment to AI's importance."

Born in India and raised in Cardiff, Narayan worked in government and business before entering Parliament in 2024 as the MP for the Vale of Glamorgan.

As Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State within Sir Keir Starmer's government, his responsibilities spanned AI opportunities, the AI Security Institute, semiconductors and online safety.

He is expected to continue shepherding some of those briefs, though now without Kendall's leadership.

"AI is likely the most significant technology in human history. Its impact will dwarf other things," Narayan wrote on X in the early hours of Tuesday, external.

"The best case for it is compelling beyond our dreams: a reindustrialised Britain, stronger national security, public services transformed for the better."

He added that, however, AI also poses real risks to the public, adding "it is right that the British public shares those worries, for jobs, for the pace of change".

Dom Hallas, head of tech trade body, the Startup Coalition, said it was key that, with the dismantling of DSIT, the government did "not take the foot off the pedal" with tech.

He said the previous department had provided good foundations - and now the priority should be spreading AI tech adoption through government and the wider public.

"The abolition of DSIT is clearly a bad thing but if anyone could make up for it in Cabinet it would be Kanishka who knows start-ups and the ecosystem better than anyone in Government," Hallas told the BBC.

TechnologyTab.title: EA FC 27: FUT leads to new age rating after loot box rule change
TechnologyTab.text:
EA FC is one of the most popular video game series in the world, and reliably tops the UK charts each year.

And as the trailer for the latest instalment of the annual football simulator dropped this week, one new addition drew a lot of attention.

A 16+ age rating.

Previously, the game had been marked as 3+, meaning its content was considered suitable for most players.

But last month the scope of those age ratings expanded to cover elements of the online experience including in-game purchases and mechanisms designed to encourage repeat play.

In the case of EA FC, one of its most popular features has come under the new rules.

Ultimate Team, commonly referred to as FUT, is one of the main modes of the EA FC series.

Players can spend money on virtual card packs containing a random selection of star footballers to build a dream squad.

It is possible to trade the cards and build up in-game "coins" without using real money, but it is generally seen as a slower and less effective way to play.

Earlier this year The Pan-European Game Information body (PEGI), announced it was overhauling its age-rating system used in 38 countries including the UK.

It made the decision to brand any game containing so-called loot boxes - "paid random items" - as a PEGI 16 by default.

EA FC falls under the new rules due to the inclusion of FUT, earning it the higher rating.

Critics have compared FUT and similar modes in other games to gambling, with recent research finding they "blurred the lines".

Electronic Arts, the game's publisher, has pushed back on the claims and stressed players don't need to spend money to participate in FUT.

The UK government chose not to bring loot boxes under the Gambling Act 2005, external, saying there was no evidence of a "causative link" to harms.

Despite the criticisms, FUT and other loot box-style modes remain popular.

According to EA's latest financial report, , externalFUT was responsible for a "substantial portion" of the $5.5bn annual revenue it made from selling add-on content for its games.

A PEGI rating prevents underage customers from walking into a shop and buying a product considered unsuitable for them.

In reality, the vast majority of video game purchases are now made digitally, although most major online stores provide safeguards.

In-game, most platforms and titles offer parental controls, and EA FC automatically restricts purchases on accounts belonging to players under 13.

Before the new rules were brought in, the decision on a game's rating was based on its content, rather than its online features.

Ultimately, the decision on whether under-16s can play the new edition will rest with parents.

UKIE, the trade body for the British Games Industry, said "PEGI ratings exist to give parents, players and retailers clear, independent guidance on the content of a game".

"The rating system is kept under regular review to reflect how games and their features evolve, and this update means parents can be confident the same protections apply here as with any other game carrying that rating," a spokesperson said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Hollie McNish tells Latitude 'myth' of virginity is too powerful
EntertainmentTab.text:
When the poet Hollie McNish lost her virginity at the age of 19, she stared at her face in the mirror for half an hour, expecting some sort of transformation.

She wondered how to stand like a non-virgin so her family would not guess, and worried her parents were looking at her weirdly across the dinner table, while they all ate mashed potato.

The word virgin might only have six letters, but not many other words carry as much power, she says.

"Virgin is my least favourite word in the English language," she tells an audience of hundreds at Latitude Festival, in Suffolk.

"Life is full of first times but nothing else is sold as being powerful enough to change our entire state of being - from virgin to non-virgin."

The concept of virginity, and love in general, are the focus of the the 43-year-old's latest collection, Virgin.

McNish, who lives in Cambridge with her 16-year-old daughter, first heard the word aged five, performing in her school nativity.

"I knew it was virginity that made Mary special. Joseph's virginity was never mentioned.

"I've always found it weird and kind of frightening the way we speak about this concept."

The question "have you lost your virginity yet?" was a recurring one with friends throughout her teens.

McNish says virginity is a man-made myth created by those in power, in times that "also spoke positively of slavery and stoning".

It has been used across cultures to control, shame, praise, and define people, especially women, she adds.

McNish hopes young people can enjoy their bodies and not feel less pure, or ashamed, by having consensual sex.

"My first attempt at intercourse was nice. It did not hurt, as rightly it should not, no matter the horrendous narrative about first time pain being some sort of marker of purity. I lost nothing except a sandal," she says.

McNish reaches millions of people through her books, performances, and short videos on social media, making her one of the UK's most widely shared poets.

She wrote her first poem aged seven, furious her family would not let her get a cat.

"My mum found it in the attic and it was funny to read back, I was insulting them in rhyme. Writing poetry has always been the way I've coped with things and worked stuff out," she says.

In her teenage years, she doodled poems in her diaries and made up verses about physics to help her remember things for her exams. "It made stuff I hated fun," she says.

But she fell out of love with poetry when she was forced to learn it at school.

"I remember reading the Seamus Heaney poem Digging, and thinking 'why are we reading a poem about potatoes'. Now he's one of my favourite poets, but it was just another subject I had to learn."

McNish could not find time to write poetry while studying modern and medieval languages at the University of Cambridge, where she stayed on to gain a masters in economics.

She describes getting into the prestigious university as "a massive deal" but she found the atmosphere strange and experienced some snobbery about her working class accent.

"Some students did make fun of the way I speak, though I didn't get as much stick as anyone from the north of England.

"I wanted to play lacrosse, because I'd gone to the only state school that played it, but it wasn't for me. When I mentioned my address, one player said she'd always wanted to meet someone with a house number [rather than a name] and another said it was cute that my mum was a nurse."

McNish began writing poetry again after graduating and started reading her pieces at open-mic nights.

"I loved reading and I loved writing, but being a writer didn't really enter my mind. I got asked to do more and more gigs and suddenly it became my full-time job," she says.

McNish has also faced snobbery in the poetry world. Her poems have been described as basic. She is often lumped in with spoken words poets (she does perform her poetry but does not write it specifically to be spoken) or even referred to as an Instagram poet.

"My poems are pretty much word for word how I'm thinking. I want people to understand them. Sometimes I wonder what I have to do just to be called a poet. I've been insulted at times but I don't take it to heart any more," she says.

Often ideas come to her while she is driving, and she will leave herself a voice note.

"I've never sat down and thought 'I'm going to write some poems today', I have to wait for the ideas to come to me."

McNish wrote one of the poems in her new collection, Call Me, after she got scared, dropping her teenage daughter at her first house party.

She asks her daughter to call her, even if she is "puking up every warning that I gave you," and asks her to "never let shame stop you reaching for your phone".

"I knew there would be vodka and I was so worried about what she might do. But then when she was seven, I worried she would play with slime for the rest of her life.

"When she was a bit older she quit all the clubs I'd made her go to but now we get a lie in and it's lovely. I realised the only thing I really care about is that she calls me when she needs me."

Other poems in the collection are about sending nudes, second-hand bookshops and croissants.

McNish says the main message she would like people to take from the collection is that virginity is "no more than an invented idea, created to insight shame and power over people's bodies".

"It literally does not exist. It is you as an individual who gets to decide what experiences in life mean the most to you, not some century-old leaders."
